1. verus! {
2. 
3. //==================================================================================================
4. // Flag projection helpers
5. //==================================================================================================
6. 
7. // The seven flag projections shared with the sibling `pde` module (`spec_present_set`,
8. // `spec_rw_set`, `spec_us_set`, `spec_pwt_set`, `spec_pcd_set`, `spec_a_set`, `spec_d_set`) are
9. // reused from there to avoid duplicate definitions colliding through the `paging` glob re-export.
10. use crate::x86::mem::paging::{
11.     spec_present_set,
12.     spec_rw_set,
13.     spec_us_set,
14.     spec_pwt_set,
15.     spec_pcd_set,
16.     spec_a_set,
17.     spec_d_set,
18. };
19. 
20. // The copy-on-write projection is PTE-specific (the PDE sibling has a page-size bit instead), so it
21. // is defined here. The enum is two-valued (`0` = clear, `1 << SHIFT` = set), isomorphic to `bool`.
22. pub open spec fn spec_cow_set(f: CopyOnWriteFlag) -> bool {
23.     f is CopyOnWrite
24. }
25. 
26. //==================================================================================================
27. // PageTableEntryFlags — abstract value (the eight control bits)
28. //==================================================================================================
29. 
30. // To a caller a flags bundle is exactly its eight paging-control bits. The bit-packing into the
31. // raw `PteWord` is hidden (the View is `closed`), realizing the encoding-independence the caller
32. // analysis demands. The single structural difference from the `pde` sibling is the OS-defined
33. // `cow` (copy-on-write, AVL) bit in place of the PDE's hardware `large_page` (PS) bit.
34. pub struct PteFlagsView {
35.     /// Present (P) bit — the entry maps a page (`is_present`).
36.     pub present: bool,
37.     /// Read/Write (R/W) bit — writes permitted (`is_writable`).
38.     pub writable: bool,
39.     /// User/Supervisor (U/S) bit — user-mode access permitted (`is_user`).
40.     pub user: bool,
41.     /// Page-Write-Through (PWT) bit.
42.     pub write_through: bool,
43.     /// Page-Cache-Disable (PCD) bit.
44.     pub cache_disabled: bool,
45.     /// Accessed (A) bit.
46.     pub accessed: bool,
47.     /// Dirty (D) bit.
48.     pub dirty: bool,
49.     /// Copy-on-write (OS-defined AVL) bit — set by `set_cow`, read by `is_cow`.
50.     pub cow: bool,
51. }
52. 
53. impl View for PageTableEntryFlags {
54.     type V = PteFlagsView;
55. 
56.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> PteFlagsView {
57.         PteFlagsView {
58.             present: spec_present_set(self.present),
59.             writable: spec_rw_set(self.read_write),
60.             user: spec_us_set(self.user_supervisor),
61.             write_through: spec_pwt_set(self.page_write_through),
62.             cache_disabled: spec_pcd_set(self.page_cache_disable),
63.             accessed: spec_a_set(self.accessed),
64.             dirty: spec_d_set(self.dirty),
65.             cow: spec_cow_set(self.cow),
66.         }
67.     }
68. }
69. 
70. impl PageTableEntryFlags {
71.     // A flags bundle has no cross-field constraint: every combination of the eight bits is a legal
72.     // value, so the invariant is vacuous. Kept explicit for uniformity.
73.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
74.         true
75.     }
76. }
77. 
78. // Abstract value produced by `PageTableEntryFlags::new`: records each of the seven argument bits
79. // faithfully and defaults the OS-defined copy-on-write bit to `false` (`NotCopyOnWrite`), since it
80. // is not a parameter (caller invariant: callers rely on `cow` defaulting to `NotCopyOnWrite`).
81. pub open spec fn spec_pte_flags_new(
82.     present: PresentFlag,
83.     read_write: ReadWriteFlag,
84.     user_supervisor: UserSupervisorFlag,
85.     page_write_through: PageWriteThroughFlag,
86.     page_cache_disable: PageCacheDisableFlag,
87.     accessed: AccessedFlag,
88.     dirty: DirtyFlag,
89. ) -> PteFlagsView {
90.     PteFlagsView {
91.         present: spec_present_set(present),
92.         writable: spec_rw_set(read_write),
93.         user: spec_us_set(user_supervisor),
94.         write_through: spec_pwt_set(page_write_through),
95.         cache_disabled: spec_pcd_set(page_cache_disable),
96.         accessed: spec_a_set(accessed),
97.         dirty: spec_d_set(dirty),
98.         cow: false,
99.     }
100. }
101. 
102. //==================================================================================================
103. // PageTableEntry — abstract value (flags + frame)
104. //==================================================================================================
105. 
106. // A PTE is the pair `(flags, frame)`. The frame is abstracted as its integer index (the
107. // `FrameNumber` View); the physical base address it yields is *derived* (`frame * FRAME_SIZE`),
108. // never stored.
109. pub struct PteView {
110.     /// The eight control bits this entry was built with.
111.     pub flags: PteFlagsView,
112.     /// The frame index this entry points at (== the inner `FrameNumber`'s `@`).
113.     pub frame: int,
114. }
115. 
116. impl View for PageTableEntry {
117.     type V = PteView;
118. 
119.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> PteView {
120.         PteView { flags: self.flags@, frame: self.frame@ }
121.     }
122. }
123. 
124. impl PageTableEntry {
125.     // The only real constraint is the frame bound, inherited verbatim from the `FrameNumber` type
126.     // invariant. It is what makes the (out-of-scope) `frame_address` total and overflow-free: the
127.     // derived physical base `frame * FRAME_SIZE` is well-defined and cannot overflow `usize`. (The
128.     // flags carry no cross-field constraint — `PageTableEntryFlags::inv` is vacuously `true` — so
129.     // they add nothing here.)
130.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
131.         0 <= self@.frame <= FrameNumber::spec_max()
132.     }
133. }
134. 
135. // Abstract value produced by `PageTableEntry::new`: pairs *these exact* flags with *this exact*
136. // frame (caller invariant: constructor fidelity).
137. pub open spec fn spec_pte_new(flags: PteFlagsView, frame: int) -> PteView {
138.     PteView { flags, frame }
139. }
140. 
141. } // verus!
142.

32. - `src/kernel/src/hal/arch/shared/mem/mmu/page_table.rs:192` — `PageTable::unmap` (present=NotPresent, all "off" flags).

38. - `page_table.rs:191` — `unmap` ("not present" flags + frame).
39. - `page_table.rs:494` — `replace_cow_frame` (flags cloned from existing PTE via `pte.flags()`, then mutated `set_read_write`/`set_cow`, + new frame).
40. - `page_table.rs:594` — `fill` (caller-supplied `pte_flags` + computed `frame`).

44. - `page_table.rs:106` — `map`: if present → entry is busy (`ResourceBusy`).
45. - `page_table.rs:181` — `unmap`: if NOT present → "page is not present" error.
46. - `page_table.rs:272` — `is_mapped`: returns `pte.is_present()` directly.
47. - `page_table.rs:635`, `:660` — table iteration: `Some(pte) if pte.is_present()` filters live entries.
48. - `identity_map.rs:640` — `ensure_pte`: if present → no-op return `Ok(())`.

51. - `page_table.rs:564` — `fill`: validates `if !pte_flags.is_present()` → reject with `InvalidArgument` before bulk-filling entries.
52. 
53. ## Trait Obligations
54. 
55. - Trait: `arch::mem::paging::TableEntry` (impl for `PageTableEntry`) — `from_raw`/`raw`
56.   must be exact inverses over the raw `PteWord` so `Table::read`/`Table::write` round-trip
57.   page-table memory. **Not in scope** here, but constrains `new`: an entry built via `new`
58.   and serialized with `raw()` (`into_raw_value`) must, when read back via `from_raw`, expose
59.   the same `is_present`/`frame_number`/flags. Callers (`write_pte`/`read_pte`,
60.   `fill` at `:595`) rely on this round-trip.
61. 
62. ## Caller Expectations
63. 
64. ### `PageTableEntryFlags::new`
65. - Callers assume: the returned flag set reflects **exactly** the seven flag arguments
66.   passed; in particular `result.is_present() == (present == PresentFlag::Present)`.
67.   The OS-defined copy-on-write bit is **not** a parameter — callers rely on it defaulting
68.   to `NotCopyOnWrite`.
69. - Callers assume: total/infallible construction (no error path, no panics).
70. - Callers don't care about: the raw bit layout, ordering of fields, or how individual
71.   flag enums are stored — they only pass strongly-typed flag enums and later query via
72.   `is_present`/`is_writable`/`is_cow` or serialize via `into_raw_value`.
73. 
74. ### `PageTableEntry::new`
75. - Callers assume: `result` stores the given `flags` and `frame` faithfully, so that
76.   `result.is_present() == flags.is_present()`, `result.frame_number() == frame`, and
77.   `result.flags()` returns an equivalent flag set (used by `replace_cow_frame` which
78.   reads back `pte.flags()`).
79. - Callers assume: infallible construction; the entry can be immediately serialized with
80.   `into_raw_value()`/`raw()` and written to a page table.
81. - Callers don't care about: internal representation or any packing of frame+flags into a
82.   word — only that the projection accessors (`is_present`, `frame_number`,
83.   `frame_address`, `flags`) agree with the constructor inputs.

85. ### `PageTableEntry::is_present`
86. - Callers assume: returns `true` iff the entry was built/decoded with the present bit set,
87.   i.e. it mirrors the present flag of `self.flags()`. Control flow depends on it being a
88.   pure, side-effect-free boolean query (map treats `true` as "busy"; unmap/ensure_pte
89.   treat `false` as "absent").
90. - Callers don't care about: any other flag or the frame value when checking presence.
91. 
92. ### `PageTableEntryFlags::is_present`
93. - Callers assume: returns `true` iff the flag set was constructed with
94.   `PresentFlag::Present`. `fill` uses it as a precondition guard, rejecting flag sets
95.   whose present bit is clear before writing any entry.
96. - Callers don't care about: the remaining flags during this specific check.
97. 
98. ## Abstract Resource
99. 
100. This module manages a **single x86 page-table entry** — the mapping of one virtual page
101. to a physical frame number together with its permission/state flags (present, read/write,
102. user/supervisor, write-through, cache-disable, accessed, dirty, and an OS-defined
103. copy-on-write bit) — and, separately, the **flag-set** sub-component. Callers treat an
104. entry as an immutable-by-construction value object: build it from typed flags + a frame,
105. query its present bit / frame, optionally clone-and-mutate flags, then (de)serialize it to
106. the raw word stored in hardware page-table memory.
107. 
108. ## Key Invariants (caller perspective)
109. 
110. - **Constructor faithfulness:** `PageTableEntry::new(flags, frame)` yields `e` with
111.   `e.is_present() == flags.is_present()`, `e.frame_number() == frame`, and
112.   `e.flags()` equivalent to `flags`.

 # Caller Analysis: `arch::x86::mem::paging::pte`
 
 ## Script Output
 
 Source file: `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/pte.rs`
 Script: `scripts/find_callers_lsp.py` (rust-analyzer LSP), crate `arch`.
 
 The LSP run reported **0 external callers** for *every* public function. This is a
 **false negative**: rust-analyzer resolved references only within the `arch` crate
 and did not index the downstream `kernel` crate references during this run. Manual
 `grep` across the workspace confirms the in-scope functions are heavily used by the
 `kernel` crate. The findings below are based on direct source inspection of the real
 call sites, which supersede the script's empty result.
 
 Crates that depend on `arch` (script header): `sysalloc`, `syscall`, `mkramfs`,
 `vfsd`, `kernel`, `uservm`, `arch-rust`, `test-kernel`, `test-mmio-fault`, `testd`.
 All in-scope call sites are in `kernel`.
 
 ## Scope
 
 Verification-order target functions (only these are in scope):
 
 - `PageTableEntry::new`
 - `PageTableEntryFlags::new`
 - `PageTableEntry::is_present`
 - `PageTableEntryFlags::is_present`
 
 ## Real Call Sites (in-scope functions)
 
 ### `PageTableEntryFlags::new` (constructs the flag set)
 - `src/kernel/src/hal/arch/shared/mem/mmu/page_table.rs:118` — `PageTable::map` (present=Present, RW/US/cache from args).
 - `src/kernel/src/hal/arch/shared/mem/mmu/page_table.rs:192` — `PageTable::unmap` (present=NotPresent, all "off" flags).
 - `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.rs:653` — `ensure_pte` (present=Present, RW, Supervisor).
 - `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/boot_init.rs:208` — passed to `PageTable::fill` (present=Present, RW from region perms).
 
 ### `PageTableEntry::new` (constructs the entry from flags + frame)
 - `page_table.rs:117` — `map` (flags + `paddr.into_frame_number()`).
 - `page_table.rs:191` — `unmap` ("not present" flags + frame).
 - `page_table.rs:494` — `replace_cow_frame` (flags cloned from existing PTE via `pte.flags()`, then mutated `set_read_write`/`set_cow`, + new frame).
 - `page_table.rs:594` — `fill` (caller-supplied `pte_flags` + computed `frame`).
 - `identity_map.rs:652` — `ensure_pte` (flags + frame).
 
 ### `PageTableEntry::is_present` (queries the entry's present bit)
 - `page_table.rs:106` — `map`: if present → entry is busy (`ResourceBusy`).
 - `page_table.rs:181` — `unmap`: if NOT present → "page is not present" error.
 - `page_table.rs:272` — `is_mapped`: returns `pte.is_present()` directly.
 - `page_table.rs:635`, `:660` — table iteration: `Some(pte) if pte.is_present()` filters live entries.
 - `identity_map.rs:640` — `ensure_pte`: if present → no-op return `Ok(())`.
 
 ### `PageTableEntryFlags::is_present` (queries the flag set's present bit)
 - `page_table.rs:564` — `fill`: validates `if !pte_flags.is_present()` → reject with `InvalidArgument` before bulk-filling entries.
 
 ## Trait Obligations
 
 - Trait: `arch::mem::paging::TableEntry` (impl for `PageTableEntry`) — `from_raw`/`raw`
   must be exact inverses over the raw `PteWord` so `Table::read`/`Table::write` round-trip
   page-table memory. **Not in scope** here, but constrains `new`: an entry built via `new`
   and serialized with `raw()` (`into_raw_value`) must, when read back via `from_raw`, expose
   the same `is_present`/`frame_number`/flags. Callers (`write_pte`/`read_pte`,
   `fill` at `:595`) rely on this round-trip.
 
 ## Caller Expectations
 
 ### `PageTableEntryFlags::new`
 - Callers assume: the returned flag set reflects **exactly** the seven flag arguments
   passed; in particular `result.is_present() == (present == PresentFlag::Present)`.
   The OS-defined copy-on-write bit is **not** a parameter — callers rely on it defaulting
   to `NotCopyOnWrite`.
 - Callers assume: total/infallible construction (no error path, no panics).
 - Callers don't care about: the raw bit layout, ordering of fields, or how individual
   flag enums are stored — they only pass strongly-typed flag enums and later query via
   `is_present`/`is_writable`/`is_cow` or serialize via `into_raw_value`.
 
 ### `PageTableEntry::new`
 - Callers assume: `result` stores the given `flags` and `frame` faithfully, so that
   `result.is_present() == flags.is_present()`, `result.frame_number() == frame`, and
   `result.flags()` returns an equivalent flag set (used by `replace_cow_frame` which
   reads back `pte.flags()`).
 - Callers assume: infallible construction; the entry can be immediately serialized with
   `into_raw_value()`/`raw()` and written to a page table.
 - Callers don't care about: internal representation or any packing of frame+flags into a
   word — only that the projection accessors (`is_present`, `frame_number`,
   `frame_address`, `flags`) agree with the constructor inputs.
 
 ### `PageTableEntry::is_present`
 - Callers assume: returns `true` iff the entry was built/decoded with the present bit set,
   i.e. it mirrors the present flag of `self.flags()`. Control flow depends on it being a
   pure, side-effect-free boolean query (map treats `true` as "busy"; unmap/ensure_pte
   treat `false` as "absent").
 - Callers don't care about: any other flag or the frame value when checking presence.
 
 ### `PageTableEntryFlags::is_present`
 - Callers assume: returns `true` iff the flag set was constructed with
   `PresentFlag::Present`. `fill` uses it as a precondition guard, rejecting flag sets
   whose present bit is clear before writing any entry.
 - Callers don't care about: the remaining flags during this specific check.
 
 ## Abstract Resource
 
 This module manages a **single x86 page-table entry** — the mapping of one virtual page
 to a physical frame number together with its permission/state flags (present, read/write,
 user/supervisor, write-through, cache-disable, accessed, dirty, and an OS-defined
 copy-on-write bit) — and, separately, the **flag-set** sub-component. Callers treat an
 entry as an immutable-by-construction value object: build it from typed flags + a frame,
 query its present bit / frame, optionally clone-and-mutate flags, then (de)serialize it to
 the raw word stored in hardware page-table memory.
 
 ## Key Invariants (caller perspective)
 
 - **Constructor faithfulness:** `PageTableEntry::new(flags, frame)` yields `e` with
   `e.is_present() == flags.is_present()`, `e.frame_number() == frame`, and
   `e.flags()` equivalent to `flags`.
 - **Flag faithfulness:** `PageTableEntryFlags::new(present, rw, us, pwt, pcd, a, d)` yields
   `f` with `f.is_present() == (present == Present)` and `cow == NotCopyOnWrite`.
 - **Presence delegation:** `PageTableEntry::is_present()` == `self.flags().is_present()`.
 - **Purity & totality:** all four functions are total, deterministic, side-effect-free;
   the two constructors never fail.
 - **Round-trip consistency (via `TableEntry`):** an entry from `new` serialized with
   `into_raw_value`/`raw` and read back with `from_raw` preserves `is_present`,
   `frame_number`, and flags (boundary obligation; `from_raw_value`/`into_raw_value`
   themselves are out of scope).
 
 ## Pre-existing Specs (from upstream verification)
 
 - Source: added during verification of module `kernel::mm::virt::identity_map`
   (file `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.spec.rs`).
 - In-module spec files `pte.spec.rs` / `pte.proof.rs` exist but are **empty**
   (`verus! { }`). No `#[verus_spec]` annotations and no View type exist on `pte.rs` yet.
 - External type specifications: `ExPageTableEntry` / `ExPageTableEntryFlags`
   (`#[verifier::external_type_specification] #[verifier::external_body]`) in
   `identity_map.spec.rs:122–128`.
 - `assume_specification` entries present for all four in-scope functions
   (`identity_map.spec.rs:170–185`):
   - `PageTableEntryFlags::new` (L170) — signature only.
   - `PageTableEntry::new` (L180) — signature only.
   - `PageTableEntry::is_present` (L185) — signature only.
   - `PageTableEntryFlags::is_present` — **not** listed (only the entry-level `is_present`
     was needed by `identity_map`; the flag-level one used by `fill` has no upstream spec).
 
 ### Assessment
 - Coverage: **partial.** Only what `identity_map` needed. `PageTableEntryFlags::is_present`
   (used by `page_table::fill`) is absent.
 - Strength: **weak.** Every entry is a bare `assume_specification` with **no
   `requires`/`ensures`** — they assert nothing about the result, so they do not capture the
   constructor-faithfulness or presence-delegation invariants the callers above rely on.
 - View design: **does not exist yet** — there is no abstract `View`/`spec` model on
   `PageTableEntry` or `PageTableEntryFlags`. The empty `pte.spec.rs` is the intended home.
   When designing it, model the entry as `(flags, frame)` and the flag set as the eight
   typed flags, exposing `is_present()` as a projection of the present flag — matching the
   caller expectations above rather than the raw-word implementation. These placeholder
   `assume_specification`s should be replaced by real `#[verus_spec]` contracts on `pte.rs`
   once verified (per the documented "placeholders removed when the dependency module is
   verified" methodology already applied to `pde`/the flag enums in this same file).

# Build Nanvix

Use this skill when the user asks to build, compile, format, lint, or spell-check Nanvix. This
covers all build-system operations exposed through the `z` utility.

## Prerequisites

- Development environment set up per `doc/setup.md`.
- A local cross-compilation toolchain (`toolchain/`).
- **Windows 11:** GNU Make on PATH, Windows Hypervisor Platform enabled,
  Developer Mode enabled, and Rust toolchain installed. See `doc/setup.md` for details.

## Windows Setup Summary

Before building on Windows, ensure:

1. **Windows Hypervisor Platform** is enabled (`Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName HypervisorPlatform -All`, then reboot).
2. **Developer Mode** is on (Settings > Privacy & Security > For developers).
3. **GNU Make** is on PATH (`winget install ezwinports.make`).
4. **Rust toolchain** is installed via `winget install Rustlang.Rustup`.
5. Repository was cloned with `git clone -c core.symlinks=true`.
6. Git hooks are installed: `./z.ps1 setup`.

## Building

### Preferred Build Commands (using `z` utility)

```bash
# Build everything with the local toolchain.
./z build -- all
```

### Building Individual Components

```bash
# Kernel only.
./z build -- kernel
# Nanvixd only.
./z build -- all-nanvixd
# UserVM only.
./z build -- all-uservm
```

### Build Parameters

Set these as environment variables or pass them after `--` in the `z` command:

| Parameter        | Values                   | Default         |
|------------------|--------------------------|-----------------|
| `MACHINE`        | `microvm`                | `microvm`       |
| `TARGET`         | `x86`                    | `x86`           |
| `RELEASE`        | `yes`, `no`              | `no`            |
| `LOG_LEVEL`      | `trace`, `debug`,        | `error`         |
|                  | `info`, `warn`,          |                 |
|                  | `error`, `panic`         |                 |

# Spec Design Guide

## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles

### Qualities of a Good Spec

1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
   `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
   functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
   exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
   copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
   verifies the copy, not the real code.
3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
   that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
   that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
   not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
   bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
   abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
   loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
   recursive spec functions.
6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
   If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
   test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
   type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
   If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
   over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
   `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
   addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
   non-negative and bounded by the address space.
8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
   writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
   this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
   unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
   directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
   (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
   `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
   vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
   implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
   and return values through the module's public spec interface,
   `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.

### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria

If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
design model.

1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
   by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
   module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
   and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
   annotation beats no annotation.
2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
   provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
   `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
   functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
   Always search vstd first.
3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
   module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
   `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
   specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
   annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
   for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
   is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
   by vstd.
   **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
   functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
   trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
   verified later, the specs become fully proven.
5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
   connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
   must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
   make Verus pass.
   **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
   with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
   can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.

### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)

1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
   struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
   signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
   Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
   erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
   prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
   rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
   genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
   
   Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
   fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.
2. **Verification Escape** — using `assume`, `admit`,
   or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
   spec or proof instead.
   
   **Exceptions (legitimate trust boundaries):**
   - `assume_specification`: for std library / external functions whose
     source code is outside the verification scope (e.g., not in our
     crate). Write the spec to match the original API documentation.

   **assume_specification Audit Checklist:**

   1. **Read the official docs first**: find the function's doc comments
      in `~/.rustup/toolchains/*/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/` using
      `grep -rn "fn <name>"`. Write the spec from these docs, not from
      reading the implementation or copying an internal helper's spec.
      Capture all documented semantics, including implicit type
      requirements (e.g., trait bounds imply properties like total ordering).
   2. **Documentation fidelity**: every ensures clause must be explicitly
      guaranteed by the original API documentation. If the doc does not
      guarantee it, mark the clause as "assumed beyond documentation".
      Conversely, every documented precondition must appear as a `requires`
      clause — omitting a precondition makes the spec unsound because
      callers will not check it.
   3. **Soft contract coverage**: identify semantic contracts that the
      compiler does not enforce but the API requires. Express these
      explicitly in the spec.
   4. **No stronger than the API**: the spec must not assume more than
      the API guarantees. Ask: "if I only read the doc (not the source
      code), would I believe this ensures clause is guaranteed?"
   5. **Version sensitivity**: note the stdlib/crate version the
      assumption was checked against.

   - `external_body`: allowed on dependency functions in other modules as
     a temporary contract placeholder (removed when that module is verified),
     and on functions pre-approved in the TCB allowed list.
     Never use `external_body` on the current module's own functions to skip
     verification.
   
   `assume_specification` and `axiom` are unverified axioms.
   See the audit checklist above when writing `assume_specification`.
3. **Missing Loop Specs** — loops need `invariant` clauses that capture
   the loop's progress and preservation properties. A function with
   loops but no loop invariants has an incomplete spec. Verus will reject
   it. For complex invariants, define a `spec fn` predicate in spec.rs
   or proof.rs and reference it in the `invariant` clause. The invariant
   must be strong enough that, combined with the loop exit condition, it
   implies the function's `ensures`. The invariant may need to be
   strengthened later — that is expected.
4. **Code-as-Spec / Operational Spec** — restating implementation logic
   or describing computation step-by-step. Bad: recursive quicksort in
   spec. Good: `is_sorted(result@) && is_permutation_of(result@, input@)`.
5. **One-Sided Error Spec** — only specifies success, says nothing
   (or `true`) about failure. Error paths need equal rigor.
6. **Missing Frame Condition / Field-by-Field Conjunction** — ensures says
   what changed but not what didn't, OR lists unchanged fields one by one
   (fragile — easy to forget a field). **Always use struct update syntax**
   (`..old(self)@`) so completeness is guaranteed by construction:

   Bad (fragile — silent field omission):
   ```
   self@.field_a == old(self)@.field_a,
   self@.field_b == old(self)@.field_b,
   self@.field_c == new_value,
   // forgot field_d — spec is incomplete!
   ```
   Good (complete by construction):
   ```
   self@ == ViewType { field_c: new_value, ..old(self)@ }
   ```
   This applies everywhere state changes appear in ensures — whether
   inline or via spec transition functions.
7. **Separate Ok/Err Conditions** — using `result.is_ok() ==> ...` and
   `result.is_err() ==> ...` as separate ensures clauses instead of a
   single `match`. The `match` form is complete by construction and
   prevents accidentally omitting one arm:

   Bad:
   ```
   ensures
       result.is_ok() ==> /* success postcondition */,
       result.is_err() ==> self@ == old(self)@,

result.content:
1. # View Design: `arch::x86::mem::paging::pte` (Page Table Entry)
2. 
3. In-scope (verification-order) targets — the **only** functions this View must
4. serve, and the only ones any later phase may annotate:
5. 
6. - `PageTableEntryFlags::new`
7. - `PageTableEntry::new`
8. - `PageTableEntry::is_present`
9. - `PageTableEntryFlags::is_present`
10. 
11. All other items (`is_user`, `is_writable`, `is_cow`, `frame_number`,
12. `frame_address`, the `set_*` mutators, `from_raw_value`/`into_raw_value`,
13. `flags`, the `SIZE` const, the `TableEntry` impl, derived `Debug`/`Clone`/`Copy`)
14. are **out of scope** and untouched. Where they are mentioned below it is only to
15. confirm the View would *also* serve them without redesign.
16. 
17. ---
18. 
19. ## Abstract Resource
20. 
21. This module models **one x86 32-bit page-table entry**: a value that binds a set
22. of **paging control flags** to a **physical frame** (the page mapped by the
23. entry). To a caller a PTE is conceptually the pair
24. 
25. ```
26. ( flags , frame )
27. ```
28. 
29. an installable / decodable slot in a page table. From it the in-scope callers
30. read back exactly one abstract fact: **is it present?** (the present bit, queried
31. on both the entry and, separately, on a free-standing flags bundle).
32. 
33. Two types need abstraction, mirroring the source structure:
34. 
35. | Type | What it is to a caller |
36. |------|------------------------|
37. | `PageTableEntryFlags` | an immutable bundle of the eight paging control bits |
38. | `PageTableEntry`      | the pair `(flags, frame)` |
39. 
40. It is *not* a collection, allocator, or state machine: both types are immutable,
41. `Copy`, pure-value tokens. Every in-scope function is either a pure total
42. constructor (`*::new`) or a pure read-only query (`is_present`); none mutate,
43. allocate, fail, or panic.
44. 
45. ### Downstream contract this View must realize
46. 
47. The verified kernel already pins the *external* contract of these types in
48. `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.spec.rs`:
49. 
50. - the types are lifted opaque via `external_type_specification`
51.   (`ExPageTableEntry`, `ExPageTableEntryFlags`);
52. - **placeholder** `assume_specification`s (currently signature-only, no
53.   `ensures`) stand in for `PageTableEntryFlags::new`, `PageTableEntry::new`, and
54.   `PageTableEntry::is_present`. `PageTableEntryFlags::is_present` (used by
55.   `PageTable::fill`) has **no** upstream placeholder yet — this phase introduces
56.   its first contract.
57. 
58. The View below is chosen so that, once `arch` is verified, the real `ensures`
59. (the spec transitions in this document) **supersede** those placeholders without
60. breaking kernel proofs. The frame index reuses the already-shipped `FrameNumber`
61. abstraction (`frame@ : int`, bounded by `FrameNumber::spec_max()`), exactly as
62. the sibling `pde` View does.
63. 
64. ---
65. 
66. ## View Types
67. 
68. ### `PageTableEntryFlags`
69. 
70. The abstract value of a flags bundle is exactly its **eight boolean control
71. bits**. Each source enum is two-valued (`0` = clear, `1 << SHIFT` = set), i.e.
72. isomorphic to `bool`; the spec-world form of "the bit is set" is a `bool`.
73. 
74. ```rust
75. pub struct PteFlagsView {
76.     /// Present (P) bit — the entry maps a page (`is_present`).
77.     pub present: bool,
78.     /// Read/Write (R/W) bit — writes permitted (`is_writable`).
79.     pub writable: bool,
80.     /// User/Supervisor (U/S) bit — user-mode access permitted (`is_user`).
81.     pub user: bool,
82.     /// Page-Write-Through (PWT) bit.
83.     pub write_through: bool,
84.     /// Page-Cache-Disable (PCD) bit.
85.     pub cache_disabled: bool,
86.     /// Accessed (A) bit.
87.     pub accessed: bool,
88.     /// Dirty (D) bit.
89.     pub dirty: bool,
90.     /// Copy-on-write (OS-defined AVL) bit — set by `set_cow`, read by `is_cow`.
91.     pub cow: bool,
92. }
93. 
94. impl View for PageTableEntryFlags {
95.     type V = PteFlagsView;
96.     // `closed`: callers reference `self@.present` etc., but the bit-packing into
97.     // the raw `PteWord` is hidden — exactly the encoding-independence the caller
98.     // analysis demands.
99.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> PteFlagsView;
100. }
101. ```
102. 
103. The single structural difference from the `pde` sibling: a PTE flags bundle
104. carries an OS-defined **`cow`** bit (an AVL bit) in place of the PDE's
105. hardware **`large_page` (PS)** bit. This matters for the constructor spec below,
106. because `cow` is the one bit `new` does **not** take as a parameter.
107. 
108. ### `PageTableEntry`
109. 
110. A PTE is the pair `(flags, frame)`. The frame is abstracted as its integer index
111. (the `FrameNumber` View, `int`); the physical base address it yields
112. (`frame_address`, out of scope) is *derived* (`frame * FRAME_SIZE`), never
113. stored.
114. 
115. ```rust
116. pub struct PteView {
117.     /// The eight control bits this entry was built with.
118.     pub flags: PteFlagsView,
119.     /// The frame index this entry points at (== the inner `FrameNumber`'s `@`).
120.     pub frame: int,
121. }
122. 
123. impl View for PageTableEntry {
124.     type V = PteView;
125.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> PteView;
126. }
127. ```
128. 
129. ---
130. 
131. ## Well-formedness Invariants
132. 
133. ```rust
134. impl PageTableEntryFlags {
135.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
136.         true   // every combination of the eight bits is a legal flags value
137.     }
138. }
139. ```
140. 
141. A flags bundle has no cross-field constraint: all 2⁸ combinations are
142. constructible (via `new` plus the `set_*` mutators), so its invariant is vacuous.
143. Kept explicit for uniformity; it adds no obligation. In particular there is **no**
144. "`cow ⇒ present`" or similar coupling — the hardware/OS imposes none, and `fill`
145. only ever *checks* `present`, never relates it to `cow`.
146. 
147. ```rust
148. impl PageTableEntry {
149.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
150.         // The frame index is a valid frame number, so the derived physical base
151.         // address `frame * FRAME_SIZE` is well-defined and cannot overflow
152.         // `usize`. This is exactly the bound `FrameNumber` already guarantees;
153.         // restating it here lets the (out-of-scope) `frame_address` be total
154.         // with no `requires`, and keeps `new`'s result well-formed.
155.         &&& 0 <= self.frame <= FrameNumber::spec_max()
156.         &&& self.flags.inv()
157.     }
158. }
159. ```
160. 
161. The only real constraint is the frame bound, inherited verbatim from the
162. `FrameNumber` type invariant. No in-scope function depends on it directly (none
163. of the four reads the frame), but it keeps `new`'s result a well-formed value and
164. matches the sibling `pde` View so the two compose uniformly in the page-table
165. layer.
166. 
167. ---
168. 
169. ## Spec Transition Functions
170. 
171. Both types are immutable; the "transitions" relate constructor inputs / query
172. self-state to the abstract result. They live on the View types (skill: reusable
173. spec helpers belong on the View, not as extra `pub spec fn`s on the exec impl).
174. 
175. ### Flag projection helpers
176. 
177. Each control enum is two-valued; project the "set" variant to `bool`:
178. 
179. ```rust
180. pub open spec fn spec_present_set(p: PresentFlag)       -> bool { p is Present }
181. pub open spec fn spec_rw_set(f: ReadWriteFlag)          -> bool { f is ReadWrite }
182. pub open spec fn spec_us_set(f: UserSupervisorFlag)     -> bool { f is User }
183. pub open spec fn spec_pwt_set(f: PageWriteThroughFlag)  -> bool { f is WriteThrough }
184. pub open spec fn spec_pcd_set(f: PageCacheDisableFlag)  -> bool { f is CacheDisabled }
185. pub open spec fn spec_a_set(f: AccessedFlag)            -> bool { f is Accessed }
186. pub open spec fn spec_d_set(f: DirtyFlag)               -> bool { f is Dirty }
187. pub open spec fn spec_cow_set(f: CopyOnWriteFlag)       -> bool { f is CopyOnWrite }
188. ```
189. 
190. ### `PageTableEntryFlags::new(present, read_write, …, dirty)` — **7 parameters**
191. 
192. Pure, total. Records each of the **seven** argument bits faithfully, and — the
193. PTE-specific subtlety — **defaults `cow` to `false`** (`NotCopyOnWrite`), since
194. `cow` is *not* a parameter (caller invariant: "the OS-defined copy-on-write bit
195. is not a parameter — callers rely on it defaulting to `NotCopyOnWrite`"):
196. 
197. ```rust
198. pub open spec fn spec_pte_flags_new(
199.     present: PresentFlag, read_write: ReadWriteFlag, user_supervisor: UserSupervisorFlag,
200.     page_write_through: PageWriteThroughFlag, page_cache_disable: PageCacheDisableFlag,
201.     accessed: AccessedFlag, dirty: DirtyFlag,
202. ) -> PteFlagsView {
203.     PteFlagsView {
204.         present:        spec_present_set(present),
205.         writable:       spec_rw_set(read_write),
206.         user:           spec_us_set(user_supervisor),
207.         write_through:  spec_pwt_set(page_write_through),
208.         cache_disabled: spec_pcd_set(page_cache_disable),
209.         accessed:       spec_a_set(accessed),
210.         dirty:          spec_d_set(dirty),
211.         cow:            false,                 // defaulted, not a parameter
212.     }
213. }
214. // new(present, …, dirty)  ensures  result@ == spec_pte_flags_new(present, …, dirty)
215. ```
216. 
217. The `cow: false` clause is load-bearing: it lets a caller (e.g. `unmap`, which
218. builds an all-"off" flag set) conclude `result.is_cow() == false`, and it makes
219. the spec reject a buggy `new` that leaks a stale cow bit.
220. 
221. ### `PageTableEntryFlags::is_present(&self)`
222. 
223. Pure read-only projection of the present bit (the guard `PageTable::fill` uses):
224. 
225. ```rust
226. // is_present(&self)  ensures  result == self@.present
227. ```
228. 
229. ### `PageTableEntry::new(flags, frame)`
230. 
231. Pure, total. Pairs *these exact* flags with *this exact* frame
232. (constructor fidelity):
233. 
234. ```rust
235. pub open spec fn spec_pte_new(flags: PteFlagsView, frame: int) -> PteView {
236.     PteView { flags, frame }
237. }
238. // new(flags, frame)  ensures  result@ == spec_pte_new(flags@, frame@)
239. //                             (and result.inv(), since frame.inv() ⇒ frame@ ≤ MAX)
240. ```
241. 
242. From this single fact the callers' derived expectations follow:
243. `result.is_present() == flags.is_present()`, `result.frame_number() == frame`,
244. and `result.flags()` is equivalent to `flags` (relied on by `replace_cow_frame`,
245. which reads back `pte.flags()`).
246. 
247. ### `PageTableEntry::is_present(&self)`
248. 
249. Pure read-only; **delegates** to the flags' present bit (presence delegation:
250. `is_present() == self.flags().is_present()`):
251. 
252. ```rust
253. // is_present(&self)  ensures  result == self@.flags.present
254. ```
255. 
256. `map` treats `true` as "busy" (`ResourceBusy`); `unmap`/`ensure_pte` treat
257. `false` as "absent". The spec is a side-effect-free boolean, exactly what that
258. control flow needs.
259. 
260. ---
261. 
262. ## Design Rationale (per field — substitution test)
263. 
264. > *If the implementation were completely rewritten with a different algorithm,
265. > would this field still make sense?*
266. 
267. | View element | Why it's needed | Substitution verdict |
268. |--------------|-----------------|----------------------|
269. | `PteFlagsView.present` | The bit both in-scope queries observe; drives `is_present` on both types and the `map`/`unmap`/`ensure_pte`/`fill` control flow. | **Passes.** Any encoding still exposes a present bit. |
270. | `PteFlagsView.cow` | The one bit `new` does **not** take, defaulted to `false`; `new`'s spec must pin it so `is_cow()` is determinate and a stale-bit bug is rejected. Read by `is_cow`, written by `set_cow`/`replace_cow_frame`. | **Passes.** A caller-visible OS attribute, independent of which AVL bit stores it. |
271. | `PteFlagsView.{writable, user}` | Recorded by `new` (constructor fidelity) and read by sibling accessors `is_writable`/`is_user`; needed so `new`'s `ensures` rejects an impl that drops an argument. | **Passes.** Caller-visible paging permissions, independent of bit layout. |
272. | `PteFlagsView.{write_through, cache_disabled, accessed, dirty}` | Recorded by `new`; complete the abstract "set of eight control bits" the type *is*, so the constructor spec is total (no flag silently lost). | **Passes.** Architectural control bits, not impl artifacts. |
273. | `PteView.flags` | A PTE is conceptually `(flags, frame)`; `is_present` delegates here, `flags()` returns it (read back by `replace_cow_frame`). | **Passes.** Any PTE binds control bits to a frame. |
274. | `PteView.frame : int` | The frame the entry points at; the inverse of `new`'s `frame`; `frame_number`/`frame_address` (out of scope) project it. Reuses `FrameNumber@`. | **Passes.** Every implementation stores *some* frame index; `int` is its representation-free form. |
275. | `PteView.inv: frame ≤ FrameNumber::spec_max()` | Keeps `new`'s result well-formed and underwrites the out-of-scope `frame_address`'s totality with no `requires`. | **Passes.** The bound is architectural (`MAX_ADDRESS/FRAME_SIZE`), not a code detail. |
276. 
277. **Why eight booleans and not just `present` (+`cow`).** Minimality asks "is every
278. field used in at least one in-scope spec?" — yes: all eight appear in
279. `PageTableEntryFlags::new`'s `ensures` (in scope). Dropping the others would make
280. `new`'s spec one-sided (a buggy `new` that ignores `read_write` would still
281. verify) and would model only part of the resource the type names ("flags of a
282. page table entry"). Keeping all eight is therefore both **complete** and
283. **minimal**, and serves the out-of-scope accessors and later phases with no
284. redesign.
285. 
286. **Why `cow` is in the View but absent from `new`'s parameter list.** The caller

 # View Design: `arch::x86::mem::paging::pte` (Page Table Entry)
 
 In-scope (verification-order) targets — the **only** functions this View must
 serve, and the only ones any later phase may annotate:
 
 - `PageTableEntryFlags::new`
 - `PageTableEntry::new`
 - `PageTableEntry::is_present`
 - `PageTableEntryFlags::is_present`
 
 All other items (`is_user`, `is_writable`, `is_cow`, `frame_number`,
 `frame_address`, the `set_*` mutators, `from_raw_value`/`into_raw_value`,
 `flags`, the `SIZE` const, the `TableEntry` impl, derived `Debug`/`Clone`/`Copy`)
 are **out of scope** and untouched. Where they are mentioned below it is only to
 confirm the View would *also* serve them without redesign.
 
 ---
 
 ## Abstract Resource
 
 This module models **one x86 32-bit page-table entry**: a value that binds a set
 of **paging control flags** to a **physical frame** (the page mapped by the
 entry). To a caller a PTE is conceptually the pair
 
 ```
 ( flags , frame )
 ```
 
 an installable / decodable slot in a page table. From it the in-scope callers
 read back exactly one abstract fact: **is it present?** (the present bit, queried
 on both the entry and, separately, on a free-standing flags bundle).
 
 Two types need abstraction, mirroring the source structure:
 
 | Type | What it is to a caller |
 |------|------------------------|
 | `PageTableEntryFlags` | an immutable bundle of the eight paging control bits |
 | `PageTableEntry`      | the pair `(flags, frame)` |
 
 It is *not* a collection, allocator, or state machine: both types are immutable,
 `Copy`, pure-value tokens. Every in-scope function is either a pure total
 constructor (`*::new`) or a pure read-only query (`is_present`); none mutate,
 allocate, fail, or panic.
 
 ### Downstream contract this View must realize
 
 The verified kernel already pins the *external* contract of these types in
 `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.spec.rs`:
 
 - the types are lifted opaque via `external_type_specification`
   (`ExPageTableEntry`, `ExPageTableEntryFlags`);
 - **placeholder** `assume_specification`s (currently signature-only, no
   `ensures`) stand in for `PageTableEntryFlags::new`, `PageTableEntry::new`, and
   `PageTableEntry::is_present`. `PageTableEntryFlags::is_present` (used by
   `PageTable::fill`) has **no** upstream placeholder yet — this phase introduces
   its first contract.
 
 The View below is chosen so that, once `arch` is verified, the real `ensures`
 (the spec transitions in this document) **supersede** those placeholders without
 breaking kernel proofs. The frame index reuses the already-shipped `FrameNumber`
 abstraction (`frame@ : int`, bounded by `FrameNumber::spec_max()`), exactly as
 the sibling `pde` View does.
 
 ---
 
 ## View Types
 
 ### `PageTableEntryFlags`
 
 The abstract value of a flags bundle is exactly its **eight boolean control
 bits**. Each source enum is two-valued (`0` = clear, `1 << SHIFT` = set), i.e.
 isomorphic to `bool`; the spec-world form of "the bit is set" is a `bool`.
 
 ```rust
 pub struct PteFlagsView {
     /// Present (P) bit — the entry maps a page (`is_present`).
     pub present: bool,
     /// Read/Write (R/W) bit — writes permitted (`is_writable`).
     pub writable: bool,
     /// User/Supervisor (U/S) bit — user-mode access permitted (`is_user`).
     pub user: bool,
     /// Page-Write-Through (PWT) bit.
     pub write_through: bool,
     /// Page-Cache-Disable (PCD) bit.
     pub cache_disabled: bool,
     /// Accessed (A) bit.
     pub accessed: bool,
     /// Dirty (D) bit.
     pub dirty: bool,
     /// Copy-on-write (OS-defined AVL) bit — set by `set_cow`, read by `is_cow`.
     pub cow: bool,
 }
 
 impl View for PageTableEntryFlags {
     type V = PteFlagsView;
     // `closed`: callers reference `self@.present` etc., but the bit-packing into
     // the raw `PteWord` is hidden — exactly the encoding-independence the caller
     // analysis demands.
     closed spec fn view(&self) -> PteFlagsView;
 }
 ```
 
 The single structural difference from the `pde` sibling: a PTE flags bundle
 carries an OS-defined **`cow`** bit (an AVL bit) in place of the PDE's
 hardware **`large_page` (PS)** bit. This matters for the constructor spec below,
 because `cow` is the one bit `new` does **not** take as a parameter.
 
 ### `PageTableEntry`
 
 A PTE is the pair `(flags, frame)`. The frame is abstracted as its integer index
 (the `FrameNumber` View, `int`); the physical base address it yields
 (`frame_address`, out of scope) is *derived* (`frame * FRAME_SIZE`), never
 stored.
 
 ```rust
 pub struct PteView {
     /// The eight control bits this entry was built with.
     pub flags: PteFlagsView,
     /// The frame index this entry points at (== the inner `FrameNumber`'s `@`).
     pub frame: int,
 }
 
 impl View for PageTableEntry {
     type V = PteView;
     closed spec fn view(&self) -> PteView;
 }
 ```
 
 ---
 
 ## Well-formedness Invariants
 
 ```rust
 impl PageTableEntryFlags {
     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
         true   // every combination of the eight bits is a legal flags value
     }
 }
 ```
 
 A flags bundle has no cross-field constraint: all 2⁸ combinations are
 constructible (via `new` plus the `set_*` mutators), so its invariant is vacuous.
 Kept explicit for uniformity; it adds no obligation. In particular there is **no**
 "`cow ⇒ present`" or similar coupling — the hardware/OS imposes none, and `fill`
 only ever *checks* `present`, never relates it to `cow`.
 
 ```rust
 impl PageTableEntry {
     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
         // The frame index is a valid frame number, so the derived physical base
         // address `frame * FRAME_SIZE` is well-defined and cannot overflow
         // `usize`. This is exactly the bound `FrameNumber` already guarantees;
         // restating it here lets the (out-of-scope) `frame_address` be total
         // with no `requires`, and keeps `new`'s result well-formed.
         &&& 0 <= self.frame <= FrameNumber::spec_max()
         &&& self.flags.inv()
     }
 }
 ```
 
 The only real constraint is the frame bound, inherited verbatim from the
 `FrameNumber` type invariant. No in-scope function depends on it directly (none
 of the four reads the frame), but it keeps `new`'s result a well-formed value and
 matches the sibling `pde` View so the two compose uniformly in the page-table
 layer.
 
 ---
 
 ## Spec Transition Functions
 
 Both types are immutable; the "transitions" relate constructor inputs / query
 self-state to the abstract result. They live on the View types (skill: reusable
 spec helpers belong on the View, not as extra `pub spec fn`s on the exec impl).
 
 ### Flag projection helpers
 
 Each control enum is two-valued; project the "set" variant to `bool`:
 
 ```rust
 pub open spec fn spec_present_set(p: PresentFlag)       -> bool { p is Present }
 pub open spec fn spec_rw_set(f: ReadWriteFlag)          -> bool { f is ReadWrite }
 pub open spec fn spec_us_set(f: UserSupervisorFlag)     -> bool { f is User }
 pub open spec fn spec_pwt_set(f: PageWriteThroughFlag)  -> bool { f is WriteThrough }
 pub open spec fn spec_pcd_set(f: PageCacheDisableFlag)  -> bool { f is CacheDisabled }
 pub open spec fn spec_a_set(f: AccessedFlag)            -> bool { f is Accessed }
 pub open spec fn spec_d_set(f: DirtyFlag)               -> bool { f is Dirty }
 pub open spec fn spec_cow_set(f: CopyOnWriteFlag)       -> bool { f is CopyOnWrite }
 ```
 
 ### `PageTableEntryFlags::new(present, read_write, …, dirty)` — **7 parameters**
 
 Pure, total. Records each of the **seven** argument bits faithfully, and — the
 PTE-specific subtlety — **defaults `cow` to `false`** (`NotCopyOnWrite`), since
 `cow` is *not* a parameter (caller invariant: "the OS-defined copy-on-write bit
 is not a parameter — callers rely on it defaulting to `NotCopyOnWrite`"):
 
 ```rust
 pub open spec fn spec_pte_flags_new(
     present: PresentFlag, read_write: ReadWriteFlag, user_supervisor: UserSupervisorFlag,
     page_write_through: PageWriteThroughFlag, page_cache_disable: PageCacheDisableFlag,
     accessed: AccessedFlag, dirty: DirtyFlag,
 ) -> PteFlagsView {
     PteFlagsView {
         present:        spec_present_set(present),
         writable:       spec_rw_set(read_write),
         user:           spec_us_set(user_supervisor),
         write_through:  spec_pwt_set(page_write_through),
         cache_disabled: spec_pcd_set(page_cache_disable),
         accessed:       spec_a_set(accessed),
         dirty:          spec_d_set(dirty),
         cow:            false,                 // defaulted, not a parameter
     }
 }
 // new(present, …, dirty)  ensures  result@ == spec_pte_flags_new(present, …, dirty)
 ```
 
 The `cow: false` clause is load-bearing: it lets a caller (e.g. `unmap`, which
 builds an all-"off" flag set) conclude `result.is_cow() == false`, and it makes
 the spec reject a buggy `new` that leaks a stale cow bit.
 
 ### `PageTableEntryFlags::is_present(&self)`
 
 Pure read-only projection of the present bit (the guard `PageTable::fill` uses):
 
 ```rust
 // is_present(&self)  ensures  result == self@.present
 ```
 
 ### `PageTableEntry::new(flags, frame)`
 
 Pure, total. Pairs *these exact* flags with *this exact* frame
 (constructor fidelity):
 
 ```rust
 pub open spec fn spec_pte_new(flags: PteFlagsView, frame: int) -> PteView {
     PteView { flags, frame }
 }
 // new(flags, frame)  ensures  result@ == spec_pte_new(flags@, frame@)
 //                             (and result.inv(), since frame.inv() ⇒ frame@ ≤ MAX)
 ```
 
 From this single fact the callers' derived expectations follow:
 `result.is_present() == flags.is_present()`, `result.frame_number() == frame`,
 and `result.flags()` is equivalent to `flags` (relied on by `replace_cow_frame`,
 which reads back `pte.flags()`).
 
 ### `PageTableEntry::is_present(&self)`
 
 Pure read-only; **delegates** to the flags' present bit (presence delegation:
 `is_present() == self.flags().is_present()`):
 
 ```rust
 // is_present(&self)  ensures  result == self@.flags.present
 ```
 
 `map` treats `true` as "busy" (`ResourceBusy`); `unmap`/`ensure_pte` treat
 `false` as "absent". The spec is a side-effect-free boolean, exactly what that
 control flow needs.
 
 ---
 
 ## Design Rationale (per field — substitution test)
 
 > *If the implementation were completely rewritten with a different algorithm,
 > would this field still make sense?*
 
 | View element | Why it's needed | Substitution verdict |
 |--------------|-----------------|----------------------|
 | `PteFlagsView.present` | The bit both in-scope queries observe; drives `is_present` on both types and the `map`/`unmap`/`ensure_pte`/`fill` control flow. | **Passes.** Any encoding still exposes a present bit. |
 | `PteFlagsView.cow` | The one bit `new` does **not** take, defaulted to `false`; `new`'s spec must pin it so `is_cow()` is determinate and a stale-bit bug is rejected. Read by `is_cow`, written by `set_cow`/`replace_cow_frame`. | **Passes.** A caller-visible OS attribute, independent of which AVL bit stores it. |
 | `PteFlagsView.{writable, user}` | Recorded by `new` (constructor fidelity) and read by sibling accessors `is_writable`/`is_user`; needed so `new`'s `ensures` rejects an impl that drops an argument. | **Passes.** Caller-visible paging permissions, independent of bit layout. |
 | `PteFlagsView.{write_through, cache_disabled, accessed, dirty}` | Recorded by `new`; complete the abstract "set of eight control bits" the type *is*, so the constructor spec is total (no flag silently lost). | **Passes.** Architectural control bits, not impl artifacts. |
 | `PteView.flags` | A PTE is conceptually `(flags, frame)`; `is_present` delegates here, `flags()` returns it (read back by `replace_cow_frame`). | **Passes.** Any PTE binds control bits to a frame. |
 | `PteView.frame : int` | The frame the entry points at; the inverse of `new`'s `frame`; `frame_number`/`frame_address` (out of scope) project it. Reuses `FrameNumber@`. | **Passes.** Every implementation stores *some* frame index; `int` is its representation-free form. |
 | `PteView.inv: frame ≤ FrameNumber::spec_max()` | Keeps `new`'s result well-formed and underwrites the out-of-scope `frame_address`'s totality with no `requires`. | **Passes.** The bound is architectural (`MAX_ADDRESS/FRAME_SIZE`), not a code detail. |
 
 **Why eight booleans and not just `present` (+`cow`).** Minimality asks "is every
 field used in at least one in-scope spec?" — yes: all eight appear in
 `PageTableEntryFlags::new`'s `ensures` (in scope). Dropping the others would make
 `new`'s spec one-sided (a buggy `new` that ignores `read_write` would still
 verify) and would model only part of the resource the type names ("flags of a
 page table entry"). Keeping all eight is therefore both **complete** and
 **minimal**, and serves the out-of-scope accessors and later phases with no
 redesign.
 
 **Why `cow` is in the View but absent from `new`'s parameter list.** The caller
 analysis is explicit: callers rely on `new` defaulting cow to `NotCopyOnWrite`.
 Modeling `cow` as a View field lets the constructor spec state `cow == false`
 declaratively; without it the spec could not express the default, and `is_cow`
 on a freshly-`new`'d entry would be unconstrained.
 
 **Why `frame : int`, not the physical address.** The address is *derived*
 (`frame * FRAME_SIZE`); storing it would duplicate state and risk inconsistency
 between `frame_number`/`frame_address`. The index is the primitive `new`
 consumes — keep one, derive the other. `int` (not `usize`) keeps overflow out of
 specs; the bound lives in `inv()`.
 
 **Why composed (`PteView` embeds `PteFlagsView`), not flattened.** The source
 binds a *flags value* to a frame, `PageTableEntry::is_present` literally returns
 `self.flags().is_present()`, and `flags()` hands the bundle back. Composing the
 views makes the "presence delegation" invariant a one-line identity
 (`pte@.flags.present`) and keeps the flags abstraction reusable by the standalone
 `PageTableEntryFlags::is_present`/`is_cow`/`is_writable` accessors.
 
 All view-design Step-4 checks pass — **Substitution** (table above),
 **Caller-only** (present + cow + frame + the other six bits are exactly the
 caller's mental model; no `PteWord`, no `FrameNumber` internals leak),
 **Complete** (constructor fidelity for flags and entry incl. the cow default,
 presence delegation, purity/totality all expressible), **Minimal** (every field
 used in an in-scope `ensures`), **No code-as-spec** (specs say *what* — "records
 each bit", "cow defaults to false", "present delegates to flags" — never *how*
 bits are packed).
 
 ---
 
 ## Rejected Alternatives
 
 - **Flags View = single `present: bool`.** Rejected: makes
   `PageTableEntryFlags::new`'s spec one-sided (cannot reject a `new` that
   mis-records the other six arguments) and models only a sliver of the
   "page-table-entry flags" resource. The extra bits cost nothing in the in-scope
   proofs yet make the constructor spec total and future-proof the sibling
   accessors.
 
 - **Flags View = `{ present, cow }` only.** Rejected for the same one-sidedness
   reason: `new` still takes `read_write`/`user_supervisor`/etc., so omitting them
   from the View lets a buggy `new` drop those arguments undetected.
 
 - **Omitting `cow` from the Flags View** (only the seven `new` parameters).
   Rejected: then `new`'s spec cannot express the caller-relied-upon default
   (`cow == NotCopyOnWrite`), and `is_cow` on a constructed entry would be
   unspecified. The whole point of a faithful constructor spec is to pin every
   observable bit of the result, including the one that is defaulted rather than
   passed.
 
 - **Flags View mirroring the enum fields (`present: PresentFlag`, …).**
   Rejected: drags exec two-variant enums into spec world; `bool` is their
   mathematical form and what `is_present` returns. Pattern-matching is confined
   to the tiny projection helpers.
 
 - **PTE View storing the physical address (`addr: int`) instead of `frame`.**
   Rejected: `addr` is derived from `frame`; storing it duplicates state and
   invites `frame_number`/`frame_address` disagreement. The frame index is the
   single source of truth.
 
 - **PTE View storing the raw `PteWord` / inner `FrameNumber`.** Rejected:
   exactly the "mirroring internal fields" the methodology forbids; it leaks the
   bit encoding the caller analysis says callers must not depend on (encoding
   independence), breaking the `into_raw_value`/`from_raw_value` round-trip's
   freedom to change layout.
 
 - **Flattened PTE View (`{ present: bool, frame: int }`, no embedded flags).**
   Rejected: loses the `flags()` accessor's abstract value and the natural
   delegation identity; `replace_cow_frame` (which clones `pte.flags()`) and later
   phases would have to re-derive the flags bundle.
 
 - **Open `view()` exposing the bit layout.** Rejected: `closed` keeps the
   encoding hidden so callers reason only through these transitions — consistent
   with the sibling `pde`/`FrameNumber`/`Table` views.
 
 - **A non-vacuous flags `inv()` (e.g. "`cow ⇒ present`" or "`writable ⇒
   present`").** Rejected: neither the hardware nor the OS imposes such a coupling,
   `new` and the `set_*` mutators accept every combination, and `unmap` builds an
   all-off (`present == false`, `cow == false`) set while other paths set `cow`
   independently of `present`. Inventing a constraint would reject legal callers.

42. /// A type that represents flags of a page table entry.
43. ///

45. #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
46. pub struct PageTableEntryFlags {

48.     present: PresentFlag,

84.     ///

103.         page_cache_disable: PageCacheDisableFlag,

275. ///

281. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]

292.

306.     ///

310.             result@ == spec_pte_new(flags@, frame@),
311.             result.inv(),

2. name: verus-constraints
3. description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Verus Constraints
7. 
8. ## Attribute Style for Exec Functions
9. 
10. All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
11. (`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
12. See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.
13. 
14. ```rust
15. // ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
16. #[verus_spec(ret =>
17.     requires x < 100,
18.     ensures ret == x + 1,
19. )]
20. fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
21.     x + 1
22. }
23. 
24. // ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
25. verus! {
26.     fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
27.         requires x < 100,
28.         ensures ret == x + 1,
29.     { x + 1 }
30. } // verus!
31. ```
32. 
33. **`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
34. - `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
35. - Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)
36. 
37. Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
38. signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.
39. 
40. ## Source Integrity (exec code)
41. 
42. The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
43. `*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.
44. 
45. Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
46. exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
47. constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
48. minimal so developers can review diffs easily.
49. 
50. **Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
51. comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.
52. 
53. The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):
54. 
55. 1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
56. 2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
57.    vstd directory broadly (see "vstd & Common Misconceptions" section below).
58. 3. If verification still fails after steps 1–2, try different proof
59.    strategies (add lemmas, intermediate assertions, split into smaller
60.    functions). If Verus reports that a **syntax construct is unsupported**
61.    (not a proof failure and not a missing spec for a stdlib function),
62.    record it in `verus-unsupported.md` with the exact error message and
63.    the minimal code that triggers it. Do NOT rewrite exec code, add
64.    `external_body`, or add `assume_specification` to work around it.
65. 
66. **The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully compatible with Verus.**
67. There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Any
68. verification failure is a proof issue, not a Verus limitation. Do NOT
69. rewrite exec code, add `external_body` — these are never needed.
70. 
71. **Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
72. `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
73. constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
74. copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.
75. 
76. - **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
77. - **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
78.   derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
79.   the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
80.   `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
81.   duplicate the definition. Write `external_type_specification` **once**
82.   in the crate/module that defines the type; other modules `use` it.
83. - **Constants**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If Verus
84.   cannot resolve a constant from another workspace module, add
85.   `#[verus_verify]` to the defining module. Never
86.   `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.
87. 
88. **Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
89. `proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
90. on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),
91. vstd imports (cfg-gated), ghost/tracked local variables (each must be
92. used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),
93. `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` struct fields (only when proof requires ghost
94. state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),
95. `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.
96. 
97. **After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
98. source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies.
99. 
100. ## Forbidden Patterns
101. 
102. | Pattern | Policy |
103. |---|---|
104. | `admit()` | Allowed during specification phase as a placeholder. Must be eliminated during proving phase |
105. | `assume(...)` | Banned |
106. | `#[verifier::external_body]` | **On current module's own functions**: unconditionally forbidden in all phases — `admit()` in a proof body is the correct placeholder during specification (it skips only the proof obligation while Verus still checks exec code; `external_body` skips everything). **On dependency functions in other modules**: allowed as a temporary contract placeholder while the dependency is not yet verified. Must be removed when the dependency module is verified |
107. | `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
108. | `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — not needed under attribute style (only `#[verus_verify]`-annotated items are checked) |
109. | `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
110. | `#[verifier::spinoff_prover]` | Banned — even if verification passes with spinoff, the proof is fragile and will break with minor changes. Improve the proof itself |
111. | `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |
112. | `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on exec code | **Cheating** — cfg-gating branches, expressions, match arms, or code blocks means Verus verifies different code than what runs. Only allowed on non-semantic items: `derive(...)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`), and imports |
113. | `uninterp spec fn` | **Banned** — all spec functions must have concrete definitions. Using `uninterp` to avoid writing a concrete spec is cheating — it has the same effect as `assume` when paired with `external_body` proof axioms |
114. 
115. ## cfg_attr and verus_keep_ghost
116. 
117. - **Do NOT wrap any Verus attribute or proof macro in `cfg_attr(verus_keep_ghost, ...)`, and do NOT guard one with `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`.** This applies to `#[verus_spec(...)]`, `#[verus_verify(...)]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`, and `proof_with! { }`. These constructs are *already ghost*: the macros erase themselves during a normal (non-Verus) `cargo build` and only take effect under `verus_keep_ghost`, so an extra `verus_keep_ghost` gate is redundant and wrong. Write them directly.
118. - **`use vstd::prelude::*;` must NOT be cfg-gated** — do not add `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`. This import must be unconditionally present so that Verus-specific constructs (e.g. `#[verus_spec]`, `proof!{}`) are properly parsed and erased during normal `cargo build`.
119. 
120. See **verus-syntax** skill for correct examples.
121. 
122. ## Warnings
123. 
124. Verus verification must produce **zero warnings**. Two most common:
125. 
126. - **Missing trigger** — add `#[trigger]` on the relevant expression inside
127.   the quantifier, or annotate the quantifier with `#[auto]` to let Verus
128.   choose triggers automatically.
129. - **Incompatible derive** — `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(Clone, Debug, ...))]`
130.   to gate out derives that Verus cannot process.
131. 
132. ## Trust Boundaries (pre-approved TCB)
133. 
134. Trust boundaries — calls to code outside the verification scope whose
135. implementation cannot be verified (hardware registers, inline assembly, MMIO,
136. FFI, std library internals, external systems) — are the external-bottom
137. boundary. Which functions are trusted is **fixed in advance** by the TCB allowed
138. list (`tcb-allowed.md`). Do NOT introduce, justify, or record new trust
139. boundaries during specification or proving: if a function is not already in the
140. TCB allowed list, it must be fully verified or eliminated.
141. 
142. Mechanisms that rely on the TCB (`assume_specification`, `external_body`,
143. `axiom`) are only permitted on functions already in the allowed list.
144. 
145. **Do NOT use trust to hide proof failures.** If a function cannot be verified
146. after exhausting all proof strategies but is not in the TCB allowed list,
147. record it in `verification-todo.md` (in the logs directory) instead:
148. 
149. ```markdown
150. ## verification-todo.md entry format
151. - Function: `Foo::bar` (file.rs:42)
152. - Status: UNPROVEN
153. - Attempts: (list strategies tried)
154. - Blocker: (describe why verification fails)
155. ```
156. 
157. These are tracked separately so they are never mistaken for accepted trust
158. assumptions. The goal is to return and resolve them — not to accept them.
159. 
160. Recording a function here does **not** make verification pass: the cheating
161. gate ignores `verification-todo.md`, and any remaining `admit()` / `assume()`
162. still fails the gate. This file is an honest hand-off of genuinely-stuck
163. proofs — never an escape hatch for giving up.
164. 
165. ## assume_specification
166. 
167. `assume_specification` provides specs for std library or external functions
168. whose body Verus cannot verify (because vstd does not include them).
169. These are **external-bottom** trust assumptions (see **spec-design** skill) —
170. unverified axioms that, if wrong, make downstream proofs unsound.
171. 
172. **Allowed** for std library / external functions not covered by vstd.
173. Follow the audit checklist in `spec-design` (documentation fidelity, soft
174. contract coverage, no stronger than the API, version sensitivity).
175. 
176. **Before writing:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
177. search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`,
178. look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.
179. 
180. ## vstd & Common Misconceptions
181. 
182. vstd is rapidly evolving — specs you believe are missing may already exist.
183. **Your training data is likely outdated.** Before concluding that a std
184. function has no spec or that a construct is unsupported, you **must** search
185. the actual vstd source thoroughly:
186. 
187. ```bash
188. grep -r "function_name" /path/to/vstd/        # broad search
189. grep -r "spec.*fn.*method" /path/to/vstd/     # spec function patterns
190. ```
191. 
192. Search broadly across the entire vstd directory — do not only check one or
193. two files. Look in `vstd/std_specs/`, `vstd/seq*.rs`, `vstd/map*.rs`,
194. `vstd/set*.rs`, `vstd/arithmetic/`, `vstd/raw_ptr.rs`, etc.
195. 
196. - **Never invent vstd functions** — verify existence in actual vstd source.
197. - **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
198. - **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.
199. 
200. ## Claiming Verus Limitations
201. 
202. **The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully Verus-compatible.**
203. There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Do NOT
204. claim any construct is unsupported, rewrite exec code, add `external_body`,
205. or use `// VERUS REWRITE`. Any verification failure is a proof issue —
206. strengthen the proof, do not change the code.
207. 
208. ### Guardrails
209. 
210. **Cfg-gating exec code is cheating.** `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` is only
211. appropriate for non-semantic items that Verus truly cannot parse:
212. `derive(Debug)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`).
213. Do NOT cfg-gate match arms, closures, large code blocks, or expressions.
214. This makes Verus verify different code than what actually runs.
215. 
216. **Anti-pattern — body duplication (absolutely forbidden):**
217. 
218. ```rust
219. // ❌ WRONG: real body hidden from Verus, replaced with different code
220. fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> {
221.     #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
222.     { /* real implementation */ }
223.     #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
224.     { /* different code that Verus can parse */ }
225. }
226. ```
227. 
228. **Anti-pattern — function duplication (absolutely forbidden):**
229. 
230. ```rust
231. // ❌ WRONG: entire function gated out, replaced with a different definition
232. #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
233. fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* real */ }
234. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
235. fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* different */ }
236. ```
237. 
238. Both patterns verify a **different program** than what ships. The proof is
239. meaningless. Find a single body that both Rust and Verus accept.
240.
